Examples [01–06](index.qmd) identify *teaching* plants — lumped resonances and a coupled
normal-mode expansion. This one identifies the **real thing**: a compiled
[`rtsfreerun`](https://controlsystems.docs.ligo.org/rtsfreerun) advligorts front-end model
of a LIGO HSTS suspension — *the same C filter numerics a control-room front-end runs*,
driven through the same channel API, under the digital twin's own seismic and readout noise.
No hardware; no method changes. The Pintelon–Schoukens loop (periodic multisine →
leakage-free reference FRF → maximum-likelihood fit → Cramér–Rao refinement) runs exactly as
it does on the teaching plants.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What makes this page different
The plant here is **not** a Python lumped model — it is the compiled `x1hsts` / `x1hsts6dof`
CDS composite (built from a `.mdl` by `rtsfreerun`), carrying the as-built `HSTS_DRV_TF`
foton cascade and a 36-state MIMO suspension state space. Because that model is not installed
in CI, this page is rendered with `freeze: true` from a locally executed cache; the figures
below are real recovery runs against the compiled model, scored against an **analytic oracle**
derived from the twin's own filter definitions (`backends.rtsfreerun_oracle`).
:::


## A1–A2 · Open-loop SISO under the twin's own noise

The HSTS drive→sensor plant is the order-10 `HSTS_DRV_TF` cascade — **five modes** near
0.67, 1.01, 1.52, 2.81 and 3.78 Hz, each $Q\!\approx\!50$, threaded with near-cancelling
zeros. We inject the multisine at the coil-driver excitation port and read the 16-bit sensor
displacement while the twin runs `ligo-india` seismic on the ISI and BOSEM readout noise.
The FRF input is the **after-actuator drive monitor**, so the coil driver divides out and the
recovered transfer is the bare suspension. *(A1 — the wiring/oracle smoke test that gates this
page — lives in the test suite; here we go straight to recovery.)*

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Run the A2 optimal-excitation campaign against compiled x1hsts"
a2 = rd.a2_recovery(seed=1, n_passes=3)
rd.bode_overlay(a2.ff, a2.oracle, a2.fit, freq=a2.freq, H_meas=a2.H_meas,
                title="x1hsts drive→sensor — analytic oracle vs P&S recovery (noise on)")
```

The recovered model tracks the oracle through every mode and anti-resonance. Because the
prior-robust first pass is followed by point-optimal excitation, the drive concentrates power
where the Fisher information is — so the parameter uncertainty falls pass over pass while the
peak drive stays well under the coil-driver limit.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Modal recovery + uncertainty convergence"
display(rd.modes_table(a2.oracle, a2.fit))
rd.convergence_fig(a2.fracs)
```

## A3 · Closed-loop — the real damping loops engaged

Now the `x1hsts6dof` composite: the bare-M1 **6×6 MIMO** HSTS state space with the
**production L1 `MC2_M1_DAMP` foton banks** closed around all six rigid-body DOFs
(L, T, V, R, P, Y), tuned to a $\tau\!\approx\!5$ s ringdown — the very loops that damp the
suspension in the observatory. A closed loop normally *hides* the plant: the sensor sees the
suppressed response $G/(1+GC)$, not $G$. The P&S **reference-based** estimate recovers $G$ anyway,
by taking the FRF against the **true plant input** — the drive *minus* the controller feedback
at the `COIL_DRV_SUM` junction. The feedback sign is load-bearing: negligible off-resonance,
it dominates exactly at the damped modes.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Drive each DOF open- and closed-loop; recover the plant tensor"
d = rd.a34(n_passes=2)
display(rd.diag_table(d))
```

With the loops closed, every diagonal element comes back as the **open-loop** plant to a part
in a thousand — the controller is cancelled, not fit. That is the whole point of a
reference-based closed-loop identification: you measure the suspension you want to model, not
the suppressed loop you happened to be running.

## A4 · The full 6×6 MIMO tensor

Opening the loops and driving each input DOF in turn gives the complete drive→sense FRF
tensor. The diagonals carry the suspension's anti-resonance notches; the off-diagonals are the
genuine cross-coupling — strongest on the L↔P and R↔Y pairs the suspension's geometry
dictates. Each per-pair FRF is overlaid on its analytic state-space element below (black line),
with the closed-loop diagonal recovery from A3 in green on the diagonal.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "6×6 |FRF| tensor — oracle vs open-loop (A4) and closed-loop diagonal (A3)"
rd.tensor_grid(d)
```

The off-diagonal elements *under closed loop* still carry the cross-loop bias — recovering the
coupled matrix jointly, with shared modal poles across elements, is the parametric MIMO fit
(the named Track B follow-on). The per-pair open-loop tensor here is the honest nonparametric
MIMO result, and the closed-loop diagonal is the controller-cancelled SISO recovery — both
against the same compiled twin a real front-end runs.
